I am reading from the Free Press. The article continues at another point:
Hitherto, the treasury board has only dealt with proposals for increases. There has never been, until now, a consistent effort made to employ the existing staff more efficiently or to reduce the civil service.
That seems to me to be a most astounding statement. If private enterprise were run in that way it would not last any time. There are two great evils in it. It not only wastes the money of the people, but it wastes the efforts of the civil servants. If this report is correct, and it is written by a man who certainly does not go out of his way to criticize the government, we are not only wasting money but we are wasting the efforts of civil servants because good new jobs are not going, as they should, to the men presently in the service.
The writer says the present Minister of Finance is turning tough, and things are going to be better. This leads me to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, a cartoon in the Winnipeg Free Press. It depicts the Minister of Finance as Hercules, and a very fine Hercules he makes. It depicts the civil service as the many headed serpent known in mythology as Hydra. The minister is wielding his sword and has just cut off the head of the Department of Justice, shown as quite small, but that is the only one. I do not

know why the Department of Justice has had its head cut off. Perhaps it is because it does not spend much. This one head has been cut off and is on the ground. But the Department of External Affairs with three heads, reaching up very high; the Department of Transport with three heads and the Department of Agriculture with one enormous head, are depicted as having their heads still in place. Up to the moment, therefore, the minister has made very little progress, according to this cartoon. According to the fable, as some hon. members may know, in the end Hercules did kill the Hydra. I am not able to tell you how many years he took to do it.
I have tried to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we have had a very unsatisfactory opening this session; that it is quite clear that much has been lost by the long delay; that the unemployment situation is entirely unsatisfactory and that the government took two or three different attitudes but pursued none with any vigour; and finally, that in the realm of economy we have this fantastic situation which I have disclosed to you by reading the extract from the Free Press. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I shall vote for the amendment with enthusiasm.

Mr. Speaker, on the very day the session opened, the member for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In an admirable speech, which we listened to with the greatest attention, he, among other things, asked Providence to grant us peace, happiness and justice. Even though this is no easy task, as far as I am concerned, I do wish to congratulate him in his own tongue on what he said and on the way in which he said it, even though, hearing me, he might have some trouble recognizing the lovely tongue of Racine and Moliere.
(Text) :
Now, Mr. Speaker, having congratulated the mover (Mr. Leduc) in his own tongue, I shall now revert to my own. I have too much respect for the French language to continue murdering it for another half hour or so. I should like to extend congratulations also to the seconder (Mr. Carrick). While I know this is customary, I do it with sincerity, not of course suggesting that those hon. members who spoke before me were not sincere. But I can assure hon. members that I have very carefully read their speeches, and appreciate the thoughtfulness and eloquence of each speaker.
Although I had the privilege of piloting through this house at the last session of parliament, on behalf of my friends of Slovak origin, a bill to incorporate the Canadian Slovak League, I still consider this to be my
The Address-Mr. Reinke maiden speech, and that being so I should like to refer briefly to my constituency of Hamilton South.
There is no doubt in my mind that you, sir, and other hon. members have heard of that garden spot of Canada and the hub of Canada's industry, the city of Hamilton, If you have not, it is no fault of my friend the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross), who has sat in this house since 1940 constantly extolling the virtues of this wonderful city. Hamilton has a population of approximately 220,000 people. The riding of Hamilton South was first established at the last redistribution of parliamentary seats, and I have the honour and privilege of being its first member. On the escarpment rising some 250 feet above the level of lake Ontario, which we call our mountain, we find a city within a city of approximately 40,000 people. From this vantage point we can look out over all that part of the city lying below with its fine residential sections, commerce and heavy industry. Then farther to the north one may view Hamilton harbour, which ranked second only to Montreal in tonnage shipped in 1953 and third to Montreal and Vancouver in tonnage shipped in 1954. Finally farther north are the Burlington canal and the blue waters of lake Ontario, and on a clear day we can see Toronto about 30 miles in the distance.
This mountain portion of the riding comprises about one-third of the population. The other two-thirds begin at the foothills and reach from Hamilton bay. In this portion you find residential and commercial sections, and near the bay front we have such well-known firms as Canadian Westinghouse, Dominion Foundries and Steel, C.I.L., National Steel Car, Firestone and others too numerous to mention.
You will realize from my description of the industries there, Mr. Speaker, that our prosperity depends upon the existence of many industries which employ thousands of people. Hamilton is a workingman's city. It is gratifying to know that Canada is governed by a party that appreciates the cause of the workingman, just as I do, having been associated with the steel industry for a number of years. I am proud that our government enacts legislation with a view to improving the conditions of the people as a whole, giving them security, improving their health and living conditions, not infringing upon their right to be free citizens nor infringing on the system of free enterprise which is part of our democratic way of life.
Although no reference was made to a tax reduction in the speech from the throne, we shall all look forward to the day when reductions can be made safely. Up to the present

Our preparedness program must go on to act as a deterrent against communist aggression or until that ominous cloud which hangs over our head has been dispelled. The Canadian people would want to pay taxes, knowing that any reduction would have to come from our defence budget, which consumes nearly 50 per cent of our tax dollar, or from our welfare program which accounts for approximately 25 per cent of our budget.
My congratulations, sir, go to the government for the fine start we have made on the St. Lawrence seaway. The appointment of such a capable man as the Hon. Lionel Chevrier to head that authority is to be commended. In passing, I would like to pay my respects to the late Robert Saunders, who was the chairman of the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission. I am sure the St. Lawrence seaway power authority will miss his help during the days ahead. We are proud to live in Hamilton. The completion of the seaway will further strengthen our prosperity and renew activity to build up our wonderful land-locked harbour.
Although the legislation was passed at the last session, I am happy to make reference to the change in the Unemployment Insurance Act which permits the payment of benefits to those who become ill while unemployed. Many of my constituents had advocated that this legislation should be introduced, and were very pleased to learn of its adoption by this parliament. My friends in Hamilton representing labour will be pleased to know that the representations that were made to us in Ottawa last year did not fall on deaf ears. Responsible groups asked for an increase in the scale and duration of winter benefits, which measure has already passed this house this session. In addition local governments, labour and other agencies have asked for greater financial support to assist unemployed workers. I am pleased that our government will take action on this matter through an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
A great deal has been said in this house about unemployment. The Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe), that great prophet of gloom, has said that before 60 days have passed 600,000 people will be unemployed in this country. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said in his speech, at page 93 of Hansard:
We are in tremendous need of the production of wealth to provide an adequate base for a proper, full-fledged social security program.
I am wondering what the hon. member referred to. Did he mean that the Bank of Canada printing presses should put on an


extra shift at the mint? Then the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) said, at page 315 of Hansard:
I am positive that those who sit on the treasury benches today know that the big problem is to equate consuming power with producing power. If there is an equation of production with consumption in terms of purchasing power and prices you will have no dififlculty, and you will solve the very grievous problems that are facing the people of Canada today.
I do not think Einstein himself could have given us a more comprehensive statement than that. "Equate consuming power with producing power." There again I am wondering what the hon. member has in mind.
I could go on quoting speeches made by hon. members of all the opposition parties. "Blast our way into world markets." "Injurious fiscal policies." "Waste and extravagance." In all these speeches I have listened to I have not heard any good, constructive advice. Their one hand does not know what the other hand is doing. They compliment the government on the public works program, the building of the causeway to Cape Breton island, the removal of Ripple Rock, the St. Lawrence seaway development; then in the next breath they suggest that taxes are choking industry and the workers of this country.
Responsible labour, or the people of Canada in general, are not advocating tax reductions. All they ask is the chance to earn a decent living. All they ask is that when taxes are levied everyone should pay his or her rightful share. I am sure the opposition would not suggest cutting the corporation tax on profits which is close to 50 per cent, and raise the tax on the smaller wage earner. I am sure they would not suggest cutting the excise tax at the expense of the small wage earner.
I hold in my hand a clipping from the Hamilton Spectator of January 22, 1955. In it I find that those seeking work in Hamilton numbered 11,361 men and 3,902 women. A year ago the figures were 8,652 men and 3,410 women. There is an increase; but the total claims paid for men and women are less than 100 higher than in the same period a year ago. As the Prime Minister explained, there is no cure-all for unemployment; but everything possible must be done to relieve the situation. I refer to another clipping from the Globe and Mail of January 24, in which the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) is reported as having said:
Is it any wonder that the government offers no adequate proposals to meet the problem of unemployment when they know and care so little about it?
If that is not an irresponsible statement I do not know what it is, to suggest that this government knows and cares little about unemployment. It is entirely untrue. The

British North America Act leaves responsibility for welfare with the provinces. After all, the federal government must consider the needs of all ten provinces. It is a provincial responsibility to heed requests made by municipal governments and welfare agencies. I do believe that the responsibility of this government is to reinforce the ability of the provinces to meet their constitutional responsibilities. The provinces must develop public assistance for those in need who are not covered by other measures. Our responsibility is to assist the provinces by helping them pay for the cost of administering these measures.
I am pleased that it is proposed in the speech from the throne to ask parliament to consider amendments to the Blind Persons Act to lower the age of eligibility and raise income ceilings. While this measure will not entail too heavy a burden upon the taxpayers of this country, nevertheless it will be a godsend to those seriously handicapped people. I am looking forward to the day when the means test will be removed entirely. Its removal would not be too much of a burden, as the recipients of this pension number somewhat less than 8,300.
I was greatly amused to hear the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, when enumerating these proposals by the government in the speech from the throne, giving credit to each of his colleagues in turn. He suggested that at last the government had heeded the pleas of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) regarding war veterans allowances. I would like my hon. friend to know that all of us to your right, Mr. Speaker, have advocated amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act to raise the basic rates as well as the ceiling on permissible incomes of recipients. I have made several personal appeals to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), as have my colleagues.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was right when he suggested that it was more important to the health of the Canadian economy to have things done, rather than to discuss in the House of Commons who was the promoter. However, there is no group more deserving than these burnt-out pensioners. I am sure they received the news with much rejoicing.
I should like now to refer to the last clause of the amendment offered by the official opposition. It is as follows:
(f) in co-operation with the provinces to develop an effective contributory plan which will assure that every Canadian will have adequate hospital and medical services.
The Address-Mr. Reinke
I am quick to admit it would be very difficult not to support an amendment of this type. I personally will rejoice the day a workable health insurance plan is introduced in this House of Commons. Most hon. members on this side will support such a plan; and you may rest assured that when health insurance legislation is introduced and presented, it will be by a Liberal government. When the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King, as prime minister of Canada, announced the beginning of the health program in 1948, he indicated that before health insurance could be established on an adequate basis another development would be essential. He was referring to a nation-wide health program. Let us then glance at the picture after six years of operation.
Since the inauguration of the national health program in 1948, no less than 650 individual hospital construction projects have been undertaken. Twenty-five per cent of these are in Ontario. Then, $60 million in federal grants have gone toward hospital construction projects, and have assisted to provide new accommodation for 61,453 patients. I do not have the figures for 1954, but in 1953 there were 300,000 chest X-ray examinations given to Canadians. I could go on and enumerate specific achievements under the national health program as they affect Canada as a whole; new services established, special drugs provided free of charge, scientific equipment purchased for hospitals and public health units.
I feel it is somewhat significant that of all the moneys allotted under the national health program for Ontario, only a little over one-half has been used by that province. As hon. members know, the province must apply for these grants. As an example, in the six-year period $958,000 was allotted for crippled children, but the province has applied for only $517,440. For professional training in that six-year period $1,233,000 was allotted, but the province has applied for only $831,862. For hospital construction the amount allotted was $23,981,816, and Ontario has applied for $15,024,099. For mental health the amount allotted was $9,789,911 and Ontario has applied for only $5,201,715. So the picture goes, and a similar situation applies in connection with tuberculosis control, public health research, general public health, cancer control and so on.

Since the vote on the speech from the throne constitutes a vote of confidence or lack of confidence in the government, this amendment has been introduced to embarrass private members on this side. The opposition know that we on your right, Mr. Speaker, are anxious for national health insurance; but I can assure hon. members of the opposition that we on this side have the utmost confidence in our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and his government.
This brings me to a point which I believe should be brought to the attention of the house at this time. On July 27, 1954, I had the privilege of speaking at a rally to which

all ethnic groups had been invited, sponsored by the Ukrainian Canadian committee. It was organized under the slogan "Independence for Ukraine." The object of the manifestation was to inform the public about the underhand work of the Kremlin with respect to the exploitation of the Ukraine and its enslavement. This enslavement has been referred to by other speakers in this house on previous occasions, and reference has been made to the fact that in 1919 the Ukraine, having escaped the czarist yoke, proclaimed a free, independent, and democratic republic. Then the bolshevik government in Moscow declared war, the red army invaded the Ukraine and along with the fifth column succeeded in its conquest.
Then followed the terrible famine of 1932-33, which took about 5 million lives. The Russian communist leaders were responsible for the destruction of Ukrainian science, tradition and learning. Both Ukrainian Orthodox and Catholic churches were destroyed. Priests were imprisoned, subjected to forced labour, or killed. To sum it all up, the Ukraine was "liberated". The truth is that communists first create chaos and prepare the groundwork for a puppet government by international and internal upheavals. That is their method in every country.
However, getting back to my story, the rally was attended by hundreds of Canadian Ukrainians who openly showed their true feelings toward Russia by displaying anticommunist banners. A few weeks later while driving from Hamilton to Toronto through a small town called Palermo I noticed a huge crowd assembled on a large picnic ground. There must have been four to five thousand people. I drove into the grounds, stopped the car, and inquired about the reason for the huge picnic. I was informed that this was a large international Ukrainian picnic, and people had come to it from all parts of Canada and the United States.
In one part of the ground set aside from the actual picnic area I noticed a rather large and impressive looking monument with well kept paths leading up to it, and upon getting closer I found it to be a large bronze statue of a man. There were two inscriptions on the monument, one in English and one in Ukrainian. The one in English read:
"T. Shevchenko-in commemoration of the 60th anniversary of Ukrainians in Canada (1891-1951)".
For the information of hon. members I might mention that Shevchenko was a famous poet of the Ukraine greatly revered by the people and representative of the culture of the day. He is regarded much as Shakespeare is regarded by the English. He was born in 1814 and died in 1861. Then
The Address-Mr. Reinke I inquired about the Ukrainian inscription. Normally one would assume the translation would be the same as the English version, but this is how the translation read:
From the Ukrainian Soviet people to Ukrainians in Canada-Kiev 1950.
The English inscription was put there simply to mislead English speaking Canadians. This is nothing new to those who know communists. The monument was not sent to Ukrainians in Canada by the Ukrainian people. It was sent to communists in Canada of the labour progressive party, and was sent by a communist government. The communists have laid claim to the United States poet Walt Whitman and the Scottish poet Robert Burns, as they have with Shevchenko.
As far as the Ukrainian national federation is concerned, it was the first organized body in Canada to fight communists and to draw the attention of Canadians and the Canadian government to the dangers of communism. As a matter of fact Saturday, January 22, was the 36th anniversary of the proclamation of the independence of the Ukraine.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that I am not criticizing that group of loyal Canadians or any other loyal group of Ukrainian or other origin. Nor am I embarking on a crusade of McCarthyism or trying needlessly to alarm this government and the House of Commons. But we do have a situation which requires a great deal of consideration.
This 22-foot bronze and granite monument was sculptured in the Soviet union. For their work the two sculptors each received Stalin awards, one of the highest awards of the Soviet union. This was reported in the Moscow Literary Gazette of March 27, 1951. It was forwarded to the national executive committee of the association of united Ukrainian Canadians from the Ukrainian society for cultural relations with foreign countries. These communists own over $1 million in property with 100 assembly halls across Canada, and they operate a $3 million insurance company and a $1 million cooperative. At Palermo they have 18 acres of parkland for rallies, picnics and camping. This is a serious affair.
We are fairly certain that an all-out atomic war with the Soviet union is not imminent. We also know that communism is sworn to world domination. This is what Stalin had to say in "Problems of Leninism" published in Moscow in 1941:
The victory of socialism in one country is not a self-sufficient task. The revolution which has been victorious in one country must regard itself

The Address-Mr. Reinke
not as a self-sufficient entity but as an aid, a means for hastening the victory of the proletariat in all countries. For the victory of the revolution in one country, in the present case Russia, is the beginning of, and the groundwork for world revolution.
That is a statement by Stalin himself. How can all this be brought about? Only by affecting small groups here and there, all under innocent sounding names. They speak about the great depression that has hit the United States and Canada. They constantly sow seeds of unrest. They capitalize on unemployment, and they capitalize on the misfortunes of their fellow men. One man in my riding, having received what he felt was unfair treatment at the hands of a government board- not necessarily this government-told me, "I am turning to communism."
Did he know what it meant? I dare say some who are in difficulty due to unfortunate circumstances might be inclined to say "Communism is better than this." But is it? Do they know they will be subservient under communism to the worst possible government domination? Do they know they will not be able to worship as they please? Do they know they can vote only "yes" or "no" for one candidate on the ballot? Do they know they cannot voice opinions against the state or its leaders? Do they know they will read only that which the state allows and listen only to what the state-operated stations broadcast?
In Canada we are spending nearly 50 per cent of our tax dollar on a defence preparedness program to stop aggression. That aggression could come tomorrow or it could come ten years from now. But rest assured it will not come from the free nations, but will come when the communists think it will be to their advantage. This has been stated very clearly in the writings of both Lenin and Stalin. When will they feel they have the advantage? Only when the communists in their insidious way have infiltrated into our governments and societies. I realize we are a long way from that situation now, but let unemployment or hardship spread and this evil would spread with it.

I am not suggesting that we outlaw communism in Canada and by so doing drive communists underground. I am not saying that we should round them all up and send them to their Russian paradise, though sometimes I think it would be better to do so. But I would like to suggest this to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), whose duty it is to administer the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickers-gill), whose department is responsible for the national film board and for the education of new Canadians in some aspects. Could we not provide money in our budgets to bring to the attention of the Canadian people the purpose, effects and results of communism? Surely if we can spend $2 billion for the defence of our democracy, we can spend some money for preventive purposes. The Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission, which now employs 104 persons in a public relations department, has a budget of $996,314 to keep the public informed.
